vignette:
At 28, David has the same job he's had since graduating-financial analyst at a mid-sized firm downtown. He's always been good with numbers; they make sense in a way people don't. But lately, the columns on his spreadsheet blur together. He catches himself staring at the same row of cash-flow projections for twenty minutes, unable to remember what he was calculating. His boss has mentioned the recent drop in accuracy twice now. David apologizes, promises to focus, then goes home and spends the evening scrolling through medical forums instead.

The trauma sits inside him like a second pulse. It began eighteen months ago, when his three-year-old daughter, Ella, was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The word "leukemia" still feels foreign in his mouth, like a stone he's been forced to swallow. He remembers the day clearly: the pediatrician's voice going flat, the fluorescent lights humming in the exam room, his wife's hand gripping his so hard his wedding band cut into his finger. They spent the next nine months in and out of the hospital-chemotherapy, fevers, transfusions, a bone marrow biopsy that left Ella screaming for three hours after the sedation wore off. David slept in a recliner beside her bed, waking every time the heart monitor beeped even slightly out of rhythm.

Ella is in remission now. Her hair has grown back in soft brown curls. She laughs again, plays with her stuffed animals, fights bedtime like any four-year-old. The doctors say she has a 92 percent chance of long-term survival. David heard that number and felt nothing inside but a cold, hollow echo.

He cannot stop reliving it. Not the whole illness, but specific snapshots: the first time he saw her bald head, the way she vomited blood one night, the look on the oncology nurse's face when she came to tell them the platelets had dropped dangerously low. These images intrude without warning. A child's cough in a grocery store. The smell of hand sanitizer. A red mark on Ella's arm. His heart races, his palms sweat, and for a few seconds he is back in that hospital room, her small body limp against the pillows.

He avoids everything connected to that time. He stays away from the pediatric wing of the hospital, even for routine checkups-his wife takes Ella now. He deleted the hospital app from his phone. He can't listen to songs that were playing in the car during those months. He stopped watching medical dramas, stopped reading news about childhood cancer fundraisers. His wife, Sara, asked him last week if he wanted to help decorate Ella's room for her birthday. He said he had work to finish and closed the office door.

The hypervigilance is constant. Every time Ella coughs or runs a low-grade fever, his brain immediately scans for signs of relapse. He checks her breathing at night, counts her breaths, remembers how the oncologist said fatigue could be an early sign. He has become an expert in body language-he reads Sara's face for hidden worry, interprets her pauses on the phone as bad news she hasn't told him yet. At work, he obsessively double-checks his own spreadsheets, running the same regression three times because he can't trust his output. Colleagues think he's meticulous. He knows he's terrified that one small error will unravel everything.

His sleep is shattered. He wakes at 3 a.m. with his heart pounding, drenched in sweat, convinced he heard the hospital phone ring. Sometimes he stays awake until dawn, replaying the moment of diagnosis in his head, wondering if he missed a symptom, if he could have done something sooner. Sara has tried to reach him-she touches his shoulder, asks if he's okay-but he feels sealed off, like he's watching his own life through thick glass. He loves Ella. He loves his wife. But the love feels distant, muffled, as if the illness burned away the part of him that could feel anything other than dread.

He went to see a therapist three months ago at Sara's insistence. He sat rigidly in the chair and said, "I don't know why I can't just move on. She's fine now. I should be grateful." He hasn't gone back. He tells himself he's too busy, that next quarter will be easier, that the numbers just need to line up right and then everything will feel real again. But deep down, he knows the numbers will never add up to what he lost-the sense of safety, the belief that the world will not suddenly collapse. He is still sitting in that recliner, waiting for the next beep, and he doesn't know how to stand up.
